newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian cen bank backs govt "EMU" deficit forecast.
newsitem.headline: Belgian cen bank backs govt "EMU" deficit forecast.

text.p: The National Bank of Belgium gave official backing on Friday to government efforts to cut new borrowing to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 and qualify for a single European currency.

Releasing a raft of forecasts for the country's 1997 economic performance, the central bank said it also expected the deficit to reach 2.9 percent, down from 3.4 percent in 1996, despite slower-than-expected growth.
The bank said separately it saw GDP growth of 2.0 percent, up from 1.4 percent in 1996, but below a 2.1 percent target used by the government to prepare its recent mini-budget.
The budget is vital for Belgium's bid to join in European economic and monetary union (EMU), membership of which will be decided upon the basis of 1997 economic indicators.

The government said last month its budget was built on a triple-safety margin: a deficit target below the three percent required for EMU membership; a "prudent" (below market average) growth forecast and a 20 billion Belgian franc cushion to prevent any rise in market interest rates from inflating the cost of servicing the country's huge debt.
The central bank effectively questioned the growth forecast, but forecast lower inflation and unemployment.
Inflation should average 1.9 percent, down from 2.1 percent in 1996 and below a government forecast of 2.0 percent.
The jobless rate should fall to 9.4 percent from 9.7 percent, the central bank said.

The European Commission forecast last November Belgian 1997 growth at 2.2 percent, inflation at 2.1 percent and unemployment at 9.9 percent. The Commission is due to release revised economic forecasts on April 23.
